newsitem.title: BURMA: Burmese police block roads, prevent Suu Kyi speech.
newsitem.headline: Burmese police block roads, prevent Suu Kyi speech.

text.p: Burmese police detained several people and blocked access to democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi's street on Sunday, preventing her again from giving her regular weekend speech to supporters.

At least four people were manhandled and briefly detained by police as pro-democracy supporters tried to gather to hear the Nobel peace laureate, who has been prevented from speaking for sixth straight weeks, witnesses said.
Traffic police and military intelligence officers manned checkpoints on the street leading to Suu Kyi's University Avenue home and barred vehicles and pedestrians from entering the road.
"You cannot go through," a man, apparently a military intelligence officer, told Reuters. "You can go other places, but for government security you cannot go past."
About 500 of Suu Kyi's supporters dispersed after a 30-minute stand-off with riot police half a mile (one km) from her house.
Despite the arrival of several dozen riot police, the crowd refused to go home unil police freed a man detained earlier in the afternoon.
"We are not afraid. We are never afraid," said one man as he rushed to join the growing crowd.
The group, which was earlier shouting "Long live Aung San Suu Kyi", then insisted on staying until 5 p.m. -- the time Suu Kyi's speech would have ended.
Some said they were hoping Suu Kyi would drive outside the barricades to speak to them, as she did on Saturday, when police stopped anyone from getting near her house.
The weekend speeches began as spontaneous gatherings after Suu Kyi was released from six years of house arrest in July 1995.

They are the only way the National League for Democracy, which won by a landslide victory in a 1990 election was barred from taking power by the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council, can disseminate information.
SLORC has declared the gatherings illegal unless held inside Suu Kyi's compound. She says public gatherings that should not have to be held behind closed doors.
The SLORC began preventing the weekend gatherings as part of a crackdown on the NLD in late September, by setting up checkpoints manned by heavily-armed security officials.
It also arrested 573 NLD members or supporters who planned to attend a September 27-29 party congress. They were later released.
